steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Real-time speech enhancement
  - earbuds, headsets, hearing aids increasingly popular -> demand for real-time speech quality improvement
  - Deep Noise Suppression (DNS) superseding conventional DSP-based enhancement
  - handles non-stationary noise, diverse background sounds
  - many real-time causal DNS models rely on RNNs
  - frequency-domain input (STFT or Mel spectrograms), one frame at a time -> encoding layer -> recurrent layers (GRU) for temporal modelling
  - decoded to time-varying filter applied to noisy input -> clean speech estimate
- Problem
  - recurrent units need a lot of computation, bad for resource-constrained devices
  - efforts to optimise/deploy on embedded hardware, e.g. quantization
  - still: same computation regardless of energy/power, input speech quality, desired output quality
- DyNNs / early exiting
  - Dynamic Neural Networks (conditional neural networks) as a path
  - adapt parameters and computational graph to the input
  - flexibility/efficiency for resource budgets, real-time, device capacities, good trade-off
  - early exiting among most promising for limited hardware
  - introduced for image classification
  - decision blocks (internal classifiers) decide when to halt, based on each exit's output (class probability)
  - challenges: no feature sharing between decision blocks -> computational waste; optimal placement of decision blocks (performance gain or loss minimisation); unstable convergence from accumulated gradients -> gradient re-scaling or mixture of training strategies
- This work
  - novel application of DyNNs to noise suppression
  - adapt nsNet2 (popular architecture) to early exiting with user-predefined constraints
  - monotonic increase in denoising with each exit stage
  - user chooses denoising/computational cost trade-off
  - automatic exiting out of scope (hard to unintrusively model speech quality in real time)
- Contributions
  - convert nsNet2 to early-exiting, architectural adaptations to keep denoising at each stage
  - training strategies: layer-wise or joint
  - evaluate speech quality and computational efficiency per exit; lower cost without degrading baseline

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In recent years audio products like earbuds, headsets, and hearing aids have become more and more popular, and they drive the demand for real-time solutions that can improve speech quality. Noise suppression techniques based on deep learning, also called Deep Noise Suppression (DNS), are replacing conventional speech enhancement techniques based on digital signal processing. This is because they can effectively reduce non-stationary noise and deal with diverse background sounds. Several DNS models, especially those that can do real-time causal inference, rely on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). These approaches usually feed a frequency-domain signal (Short-time Fourier Transform (STFT) or Mel spectrograms) one frame at a time into an encoding layer and one or more recurrent layers like Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), which gives temporal sequence modelling abilities. Then this internal representation is decoded to form a time-varying filter, and the filter is applied to the noisy input to get a clean speech estimate.

But these architectures are not really suited for resource-constrained devices because the recurrent units need a lot of computation. Several efforts have tried to optimise and deploy recurrent models on embedded hardware with techniques like quantization. But one fundamental aspect is still not addressed: the model needs the same amount of computation no matter the energy/power requirements, the initial speech quality of the input signal, and the desired output speech quality.

- DyNNs (conditional neural networks) as a path; adapt parameters and computational graph to input; flexibility for resource budgets, real-time requirements, device capacities
- early exiting promising for limited hardware; introduced for image classification; decision blocks (internal classifiers) halt computation based on exit output
- challenges: no feature sharing -> computational waste; placement of decision blocks; unstable convergence -> gradient re-scaling, mixture of training strategies
- this work: DyNNs for noise suppression; nsNet2 with early exits, user-predefined constraints; monotonic improvement per exit; user picks trade-off; automatic exiting out of scope
- contributions: conversion + architectural adaptations; layer-wise vs joint training; evaluation of speech quality and efficiency per exit

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In recent years audio products like earbuds, headsets, and hearing aids have become more and more popular, and they drive the demand for real-time solutions that can improve speech quality. Noise suppression techniques based on deep learning, also called Deep Noise Suppression (DNS), are replacing conventional speech enhancement techniques based on digital signal processing. This is because they can effectively reduce non-stationary noise and deal with diverse background sounds. Several DNS models, especially those that can do real-time causal inference, rely on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs). These approaches usually feed a frequency-domain signal (Short-time Fourier Transform (STFT) or Mel spectrograms) one frame at a time into an encoding layer and one or more recurrent layers like Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), which gives temporal sequence modelling abilities. Then this internal representation is decoded to form a time-varying filter, and the filter is applied to the noisy input to get a clean speech estimate.

But these architectures are not really suited for resource-constrained devices because the recurrent units need a lot of computation. Several efforts have tried to optimise and deploy recurrent models on embedded hardware with techniques like quantization. But one fundamental aspect is still not addressed: the model needs the same amount of computation no matter the energy/power requirements, the initial speech quality of the input signal, and the desired output speech quality.

One path to deal with this issue is Dynamic Neural Networks (DyNNs), also called conditional neural networks. DyNNs can adjust their parameters and also their computational graph adaptively, depending on the input they get. This gives the network more flexibility and efficiency for handling different resource budgets, real-time requirements, and device capacities, and it keeps a good performance trade-off. One of the most promising DyNN techniques that seems suitable for limited hardware resources is early exiting. Early exiting was introduced for image classification. It adds decision blocks (e.g., internal classifiers) to the architecture, and they decide when to stop the computations based on the output of each exit stage (e.g., image class probability). This way the full network does not have to be used, but these new types of architectures have various challenges. For example, if internal decision blocks do not share features this can lead to computational waste. Another challenge is where to place the decision blocks in the architecture, based on either performance gain or loss minimisation. Also, convergence can be unstable because gradients from the different decision blocks accumulate, and this can be mitigated by gradient re-scaling or a mixture of training strategies.

In this work we introduce a new application of DyNNs to noise suppression. We adapt nsNet2, which is a popular architecture for noise suppression, into a model that can exit early given user-predefined constraints. We then show that the resulting architecture's denoising capabilities increase monotonically with each consecutive exit stage. The user can choose the denoising/computational cost trade-off that suits them best. Automatic exiting is beyond the scope of this work, because of the additional challenges of modelling speech quality unintrusively in real-time. In this paper:

- • We convert nsNet2 into an early-exiting model and try several architectural adaptations to keep its denoising capabilities at each stage;

- • We look at the impact of different early exit training strategies (layer-wise or joint) on the denoising performance of the models;

- • We evaluate speech quality and computational efficiency of our models at each exit stage and show that our architectural adaptations decrease computational cost without degrading baseline performances.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In recent years, audio products such as earbuds, headsets, and hearing aids have become increasingly popular and are driving the demand for real-time solutions that can improve speech quality. Noise suppression techniques based on deep learning — also referred to as Deep Noise Suppression (DNS) — are superseding conventional speech enhancement techniques based on digital signal processing, thanks to their ability to effectively reduce non-stationary noise and deal with diverse background sounds. Several DNS models, in particular those capable of real-time causal inference, rely on Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) [1,2,3]. Such approaches usually feed a frequency-domain signal — in the form of Short-time Fourier Transform (STFT) or Mel spectrograms — one frame at a time into an encoding layer and one or more recurrent layers such as Gated Recurrent Units (GRU), which provides temporal sequence modelling abilities. This internal representation is then decoded to form a time-varying filter, which is applied to the noisy input to obtain a clean speech estimate.

Unfortunately, such architectures are not well suited for resource-constrained devices due to the large amount of computation required by the recurrent units. Several efforts have been made to optimise and deploy recurrent models on embedded hardware [4,5] with techniques such as quantization. Nevertheless, one fundamental aspect remains unaddressed: the model requires the same amount of computation irrespective of energy/power requirements, initial speech quality of the input signal, and desired output speech quality.

To address this issue, Dynamic Neural Networks (DyNNs), also known as conditional neural networks, are one path to follow [6]. DyNNs can adaptively adjust their parameters as well as their computational graph, based on the input they receive. This dynamism gives the network more flexibility and efficiency in handling various resource budgets, real-time requirements, and device capacities while maintaining a good performance trade-off. Among the most promising DyNN techniques for addressing limited hardware resources is early exiting [7,8,9]. Early exiting was introduced in the context of image classification [10,11]. It appends decision blocks (e.g., internal classifiers) to the architecture, which decide when to halt the computations based on the output of each exit stage (e.g., image class probability). This paradigm avoids using the full-fledged network, but various challenges emerge from these new types of architectures. For instance, the absence of feature sharing between internal decision blocks can lead to computational waste [12,13]. Another challenge lies in the optimal placement of the decision blocks in the architecture based on either performance gain or loss minimisation [14,15]. Moreover, convergence can be unstable due to the accumulation of gradients coming from the different decision blocks, which can be mitigated by gradient re-scaling [16] or a mixture of training strategies [17].

In this work, we introduce a novel application of DyNNs to noise suppression. We adapt nsNet2 [1], a popular architecture for noise suppression, into a model capable of early exiting given user-predefined constraints. We then show that the resulting architecture achieves a monotonic increase in its denoising capabilities with each consecutive exit stage, allowing the user to choose the denoising/computational cost trade-off that best suits their needs. Due to the additional challenges of unintrusively modelling speech quality in real-time, automatic exiting is beyond the scope of this work. In this paper:

- • We convert nsNet2 into an early-exiting model and explore several architectural adaptations aimed at maintaining its denoising capabilities at each stage;

- • We investigate the impact of different early exit training strategies (layer-wise or joint) on the denoising performance of the models;

- • We evaluate the speech quality and computational efficiency of our models for each exit stage and show that our architectural adaptations decrease computational cost without degrading baseline performances.
